critiques.title: Use one legend that explains both species and trend status
critiques.issue: The trend chart encodes species with both color and stroke pattern, but it exposes separate legends for color and strokeDash, forcing readers to reconcile two parallel keys for the same lines.
critiques.rationale: A single combined legend is easier to scan and better supports the requirement not to rely on color alone. Right now the redundant cue exists, but its explanation is fragmented across duplicate legends.
critiques.evidence: population-trend uses color and strokeDash on the same bird field, and both encodings have their own visible legends oriented top-right.
critiques.suggestion: Keep the dashed/solid distinction, but remove the extra stroke-dash legend so one legend carries the species labels while the line patterns remain visible on the marks themselves.

critiques.title: Use line style for decline status and reserve color for species identity
critiques.issue: The trend chart uses both color and strokeDash by species, but the panel copy asks readers to interpret dashed lines as long-term decline. Because dash is currently tied to bird identity, the visual encoding does not cleanly separate species from status.
critiques.rationale: Readers need to see two meanings at once in this panel: which species each line represents and which trajectories are in decline. Encoding both channels with species makes the 'dashed means decline' message harder to verify and less accessible.
critiques.evidence: The color scale maps bird to three colors, and strokeDash also maps bird with House Sparrow and Starling dashed while Blue Tit is solid.
critiques.suggestion: Compute decline status from each bird’s 2023 index, then map strokeDash to that derived status while preserving color by bird.

critiques.title: Include the latest year on the time axis

critiques.title: Use one typographic system across the board
critiques.issue: The dashboard mixes serif and sans-serif fonts across the board title, subtitle, and chart specs, which weakens the cohesive editorial feel and conflicts with the supplied BBC typography direction.
critiques.rationale: Narrative infographics rely on a polished, unified voice. Here the title uses Georgia, the subtitle uses system-ui, one chart uses Palatino/Georgia, and another uses Arial, so the board reads as assembled from separate styles rather than one story package.
critiques.evidence: board.typography shows Georgia for the title and system-ui for the subtitle; birds-ranking and did-you-know use Palatino/Georgia in spec config, while population-trend uses Arial/Helvetica.
critiques.suggestion: Apply a single BBC Reith-based font family across the board and all tiles to create a consistent editorial system.
